title: Basic Input Validation
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of basic input validation and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—checking empty input—in a small, readable example.
Predict the example result and check it against the stated output or a boundary-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study basic input validation with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you turn raw console input into validated data and provide clear feedback for invalid values. In this lesson, focus on checking empty input and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat console input as untrusted text. Validate format and range before using it, account for token-versus-line reading, and give users a clear way to correct invalid input. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect checking empty input with validating numeric input before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Checking acceptable ranges
items.text: Console input is external data. Distinguish token-reading from line-reading, validate parsed values and ranges, and make malformed or missing input produce a clear response. Apply that reasoning specifically to checking acceptable ranges and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

content.task: Try it yourself: build the smallest program that demonstrates checking empty input. Change one input, predict the result, and add one boundary or invalid case before considering the task complete.

common_mistakes.problem: Applying the rule from memory without checking its exact contract.
common_mistakes.why: Small differences in type, scope, API version, or input shape can change the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the relevant official API/language documentation and build a minimal reproducer.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.
